name: Classic Rock
about: Classic rock is less a style than a canon: the guitar-driven, album-oriented rock made roughly between 1965 and the mid-1980s that American FM radio codified into a format in the early 1980s. The sound is big and analogue, built on riffs, extended solos, Hammond organ, blues and folk roots and singers who could fill a hall, with the LP rather than the single as the unit of ambition. Led Zeppelin, the Rolling Stones and the Who sit at the centre, with Pink Floyd, the Eagles, Fleetwood Mac, Tom Petty and AC/DC filling out the playlist. The format has barely changed in forty years, which is both its appeal and its problem: these records remain among the best-selling and most-played in rock, and the term now covers anything old enough to feel settled.

artists.name: The Rolling Stones
artists.why: blues, swagger and the long run

artists.name: Eagles
artists.why: California country rock at its most polished

artists.name: Creedence Clearwater Revival
artists.why: swamp rock, one hit after another

artists.name: Bruce Springsteen
artists.why: working-class epics with the E Street Band

albums.title: The Doors
albums.why: Organ-led blues, Morrison's baritone and an eleven-minute Oedipal finale made this the most dramatic debut of the Los Angeles 1960s.

albums.title: Electric Ladyland
albums.why: Hendrix's sprawling double album, from the fifteen-minute blues jam to the definitive Dylan cover, is as far as he took the studio.

albums.title: Abbey Road
albums.why: The Beatles' last recorded album is their most polished, with George Harrison's two best songs and a side-two medley nobody has bettered.

albums.title: Led Zeppelin II
albums.why: Written and recorded on the road, with the riffs that defined hard rock and Bonham's drums louder than anyone had dared before.

albums.title: Cosmo's Factory
albums.why: Fogerty's swamp rock at its most complete, pairing three-minute hits with an eleven-minute Marvin Gaye cover that earns its length.

albums.title: Layla and Other Assorted Love Songs
albums.why: Clapton and Duane Allman trading guitar lines over an album of romantic desperation; the title track still justifies its reputation.

albums.title: At Fillmore East
albums.why: The live album as peak statement, with twin guitars and two drummers stretching the blues into long-form improvisation without losing the groove.

albums.title: Who's Next
albums.why: Salvaged from the abandoned Lifehouse project, the Who's most muscular record pairs early synthesizers with Townshend's biggest power chords.

albums.title: Sticky Fingers
albums.why: The first full album with Mick Taylor, where the Stones' country, blues and soul sides came together with their sharpest playing.

albums.title: Machine Head
albums.why: Recorded in a Montreux hotel corridor, the album with the most-learned riff in rock and Deep Purple's most disciplined set of songs.

albums.title: (Pronounced 'Lĕh-'nérd 'Skin-'nérd)
albums.why: Three guitars, Ronnie Van Zant's plain-spoken songs and a nine-minute closer that became Southern rock's anthem, all on a debut.

albums.title: Wish You Were Here
albums.why: A tribute to Syd Barrett and an attack on the music business, built around a two-part suite that is Gilmour's finest hour.

albums.title: A Night at the Opera
albums.why: Queen's most extravagant record, where vaudeville, hard rock and a six-minute mock opera somehow belong on the same side of vinyl.

albums.title: Rocks
albums.why: Aerosmith at their rawest and most confident, a hard rock record of swing and sleaze that the next generation of metal bands studied closely.

albums.title: Boston
albums.why: Tom Scholz's basement-built debut defined the sound of American arena rock radio and sold as if it had been designed to.

albums.title: Hotel California
albums.why: The Eagles' cynical portrait of 1970s California, impeccably produced and sung, and still the format's most-played album.

albums.title: Rumours
albums.why: Two couples breaking up in the same band produced the most immaculate pop-rock record of the decade and one of the biggest sellers ever.

albums.title: Aja
albums.why: Jazz-schooled session players, cryptic lyrics and perfectionist production; the sound of 1970s studio rock at its most sophisticated.

albums.title: Van Halen
albums.why: The debut that introduced Eddie Van Halen's tapping and Roth's showmanship, resetting what a hard rock guitar record could sound like.

albums.title: Darkness on the Edge of Town
albums.why: Leaner and angrier than Born to Run, with the songs about work and disappointment that gave Springsteen his adult subject.

albums.title: Damn the Torpedoes
albums.why: Petty's breakthrough, where Jimmy Iovine's production and a run of radio hits turned Byrds-style jangle into American arena rock.

albums.title: Back in Black
albums.why: Recorded months after Bon Scott's death, with Brian Johnson's first vocals and ten riffs that have never left rock radio.

albums.title: Moving Pictures
albums.why: Rush's progressive instincts trimmed to radio length, with synths, reggae turns and the drum part every rock drummer learns.

albums.title: Brothers in Arms
albums.why: The album that sold the CD player, with Knopfler's clean guitar and a few songs much better than its coffee-table reputation suggests.
